classification_signals: The paper is structured into multiple 'EXPERIMENT' sections (Experiment 1-5), each with 'Method', 'Subjects', 'Stimuli', 'Apparatus', 'Design', 'Procedure', and 'Results and Discussion' subsections (e.g., p. 412, 414, 418, 420, 423).

It describes controlled manipulations (e.g., viewing hills from base vs. top, real vs. virtual reality, before vs. after fatiguing exercise) and measures (verbal estimates, visual matching, haptic adjustments) (e.g., p. 412, 414, 418, 423).
Statistical analyses such as t-tests, ANOVA, and regression with p-values and effect sizes (R², exponents) are reported for each experiment (e.g., p. 413, 416, 419, 421, 424).

limitations: It is not known whether the influence of viewpoint on the haptic measure was due to differential ease in adjusting the palm board across the two viewpoints, or to the effect of some variable that caused a genuine change in haptic perception (p. 418).

The authors acknowledge an alternative explanation for the fatigue effect (that visually guided actions were recalibrated throughout the runners' excursions) but state they have no evidence against it, though they find it less plausible than the separate visual systems account (p. 426).
minimum_safe_summary: This empirical study investigated the perception of geographical slant using verbal, visual, and haptic measures across five experiments. Key findings include a consistent overestimation of hill steepness in verbal and visual reports, but accurate judgments via haptic adjustments. Perceived steepness was influenced by viewpoint (steeper from the top for steeper hills) and physical fatigue (steeper when tired), supporting the idea that slant perception relates to behavioral potential (affordances). The authors propose that the dissociation between conscious perception and visually guided action is due to separate visual pathways and calibration mechanisms. Limitations include uncertainty about the exact cause of viewpoint effects on haptic judgments and the inability to definitively rule out alternative explanations for fatigue effects.

instruments_used.name: Visual matching
instruments_used.description: Participants adjust a visual display (e.g., a line on a protractor, a tiltable board) to match the perceived slant of the hill.

instruments_used.name: Haptic matching
instruments_used.description: Participants adjust a haptic device (e.g., a board manipulated by hand, out of sight) to match the perceived slant of the hill.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: The perception of geographical slant is not purely optical but is scaled by the observer's physiological state, capabilities, and the effort required to act upon the environment (e.g., climb the hill).

mechanism_chain.description: The mechanism by which an observer's physiological state and perceived effort influence the perception of geographical slant.
